newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mine royalty, end to depletion plan proposed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mine royalty, end to depletion plan proposed.

text.p: Two senior lawmakers, making good on a proposal in President Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget plan, filed a bill Thursday to charge a 5 percent royalty on hard rock minerals extracted from public land.
They also filed companion bills to end the depletion allowance for mineral operations on public land, to charge a mine reclamation fee and to make permanent the filing fees now charged on claims.
Clinton asked for extension of the annual fees, $100 for existing claims and $125 for new ones, which were due to expire in 1998.

Congress has wrangled for years over revisions to the 1872 mining law, which controls hard rock mining on public lands. Repeated attempts to impose a royalty have failed. Hard rock minerals include copper, silver and gold.

Altogether, the royalties, claim maintenance fees, reclamation fees and elimination of the depletion allowance would save $1.5 billion over five years, sponsors estimated. The bills were filed by Rep. George Miller of California and Sen. Dale Bumpers of Arkansas, the Democratic leaders on the House and Senate committees that oversee public lands. Republicans control both chambers.
"Overhaul of the mining law is long overdue," Miller said. "These bill will finally begin to give a fair return to the taxpayer and restore despoiled public lands."
Under the royalty bill, the government would end the land patent system that allows sale of public land through a mining claim for as little as $2.50 an acre.
The royalty rate would be 5 percent of the net smelter return on production of minerals on claims located under the 1872 Mining Act.
A fee of 2 percent to 5 percent of net income would be assessed for reclamation of abandoned hardrock mines. The sliding scale fee would be based on a mine's profitability.
Bumpers described the 1872 law as antiquated and said it "gouges the taxpayers and forfeits our stewardship over millions of acres of public land and precious resources."
Westerners have fought the royalty proposals as part of a "war on the West" that would destroy an important industry.

Miller and Bumpers estimated the royalties would generate $175 million over five years, the reclamation fee $750 million and the claim fees $135 million. Ending the depletion allowance would save the Treasury $468 million in the same period.
